blocks.title: Principle of crystallization
blocks.text: The solute should be soluble in a suitable solvent at high temperature, and the excess solute is thrown out as crystals when the solution is cooled.

items: It should dissolve a large amount of the substance at its boiling point and only a small amount at room temperature.
It should not react chemically with the solute.
It should either not dissolve the impurities, or the impurities should not crystallize from it along with the solute.
On cooling it should deposit well-formed crystals of the pure compound.
It should be inexpensive, safe to use and easily removable.

blocks.text: The solvents most used are water, absolute ethanol, chloroform, carbon tetrachloride and acetic acid; if none is suitable, a combination of two or more miscible solvents may be used. If the solvent is inflammable, the solution is heated on a water bath so that it does not catch fire. If crystals start to appear during the hot filtration they choke the filter paper or funnel; a hot-water funnel avoids this.

blocks.prompt: Why is there a need to crystallize a crude product, and how is a suitable solvent selected (exercise Q.2a; Quick Check 15.2a, b; Q.4)?
blocks.explanation: A crude product carries unreacted starting material and by-products; crystallization leaves these in the mother liquor and gives a pure solid. The solvent is chosen so that the compound dissolves abundantly when hot and sparingly when cold, does not react with it, leaves impurities either undissolved or in solution, gives good crystals, and is cheap, safe and easily removed; water, ethanol, chloroform, carbon tetrachloride and acetic acid are the usual choices.

items: Crystallization: dissolve hot, cool to throw out crystals. Ideal solvent: much solute hot, little cold; no reaction; impurities left behind; good crystals; cheap, safe, removable (water, ethanol, chloroform, CCl4, acetic acid; mixed solvents; water bath for inflammable solvents; hot-water funnel).
